question: What is the literal meaning of the medical term neoplasm?
explanation: The term neoplasm comes from Greek roots meaning new formation or growth, which describes the abnormal tissue mass formed by runaway cell division. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why do neoplastic cells form a tumor instead of behaving normally?

options.A: They expand rapidly because they are fighting off local infections
options.B: They grow larger to replace dead tissue in the organ
options.C: They absorb too much water from surrounding blood vessels
options.D: They multiply uncontrollably due to failed growth regulation

explanation: You've got this! Normally, our body tells cells when to rest and when to divide. In a tumor, those control signals fail, and the cells just keep multiplying without stopping. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which feature is typical of a benign tumor?

options.B: It is enclosed by a fibrous capsule
options.C: It looks completely different from normal cells
options.D: It spreads quickly through the bloodstream

explanation: Benign growths typically form a distinct capsule that separates them from surrounding tissue, making them easier to excise. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h2)

question: Even though a benign tumor is non-cancerous, why can it still be dangerous to a patient?

options.A: It always releases toxic poisons into the bloodstream
options.B: It can press on vital structures inside confined spaces
options.C: It frequently turns into widespread blood cancer
options.D: It destroys the immune system completely

explanation: Think about a crowded room! Even if things are peaceful, if a tumor grows inside a tight space like the skull, it can press on vital organs and cause serious trouble. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is the term for cancer cells spreading to distant parts of the body?
explanation: Metastasis occurs when malignant cells break free, enter circulation or lymph channels, and establish secondary tumor sites far from the original growth. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h3)

question: Why do fast-growing malignant tumors encourage angiogenesis (the growth of new blood vessels)?

options.A: It causes the tumor cells to mature and look normal
options.B: It stops the tumor from spreading to other organs
options.C: It helps cancer cells hide from white blood cells
options.D: It creates new blood vessels to supply oxygen and nutrients

explanation: Clever! Tumors need food and oxygen to keep growing rapidly. By triggering angiogenesis, they force the body to build a dedicated supply line straight to them. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h3)

question: What do we call a cancer that starts in the epithelial tissue lining body surfaces?
explanation: You're doing great! Carcinomas are the most common type of cancer because they start in the skin and the cells lining our internal organs and body surfaces. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h4)

question: A patient is diagnosed with a tumor growing in the smooth muscle of the thigh. Which classification applies best?
explanation: Connective and supportive tissues like muscle, bone, and fat give rise to sarcomas rather than carcinomas. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h4)

question: What does the 'T' stand for in the TNM cancer staging system?
explanation: In the TNM system, T evaluates the size and direct extent of the primary tumor, N assesses lymph node involvement, and M checks for distant metastasis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h5)

question: How is cancer grading different from cancer staging?

options.A: Grading counts white blood cells, while staging counts red blood cells
options.B: Grading is only used for benign tumors, while staging is for malignant ones
options.C: Grading looks at cellular appearance under a microscope, while staging looks at how far the cancer has spread
options.D: Grading measures organ failure, while staging measures treatment success

explanation: Think of it this way: Grading checks how 'wild' or abnormal the cells look under a microscope, while staging looks at the map of the body to see how far the cancer has traveled. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a common side effect of chemotherapy that nurses watch out for?
explanation: You've got this! Encapsulation is a trait of benign, harmless-looking growths, not a side effect of chemo. Chemo hits fast-dividing cells, which often leads to fatigue and low blood counts. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h6)

question: A patient on chemotherapy has a very low white blood cell count. What should be your top nursing priority?

options.A: Administering high doses of oral iron supplements
options.B: Encouraging heavy physical exercise to combat fatigue
options.C: Preparing the patient for immediate surgical tumor removal
options.D: Protecting the patient from potential sources of infection

explanation: Brilliant nursing logic! White blood cells are our body's soldiers. When their count drops (neutropenia), our main job is to guard the patient fiercely against any germs and infections. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h6)
